title: Bear one another's burdens (Galatians 6:2)
hookLine: carrying each other's loads is how the law of Christ is kept
last: HOW IS IT WITH YOUR SOUL?

cards: Moving day. You've boxed up your whole life, and the couch is at the bottom of three flights of stairs. Alone, it's impossible; you'd wreck your back and the wall.

Then two friends show up, one on each end, and suddenly it's awkward, funny and done in ten minutes. The same weight, split, becomes something else. Paul, writing to the churches in Galatia, reaches for that picture.
He's argued for five chapters about rules and freedom, and near the end he gives an instruction that sounds a lot like moving day.

teach.h: THE LAW OF CHRIST: CARRY EACH OTHER.
teach.b: In the King James Bible: "Bear ye one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ." The Galatians have been arguing about which laws Christians must keep. And Paul says: you want a law?
Here's the law of Christ. Carry each other. Not a new rulebook.
Love you can lift. Now, a puzzle.
Three verses later, Paul seems to say the opposite: "For every man shall bear his own burden." Which is it? The answer is in the Greek.
In verse two, the word for burdens means heavy weights, crushing loads nobody should carry alone.

teach.h: A CRUSHING WEIGHT, AND A DAILY PACK.
teach.b: In verse five it's a different word, a load or a pack, which some readers picture as the kit a soldier carries on a march: your own daily load. Paul means both. Carry your own pack: do your own work, own your own choices.
And when someone is crushed by a weight too heavy for one person, a grief, an illness, a debt, a failure, get under it with them.
The verse just before says who does the lifting: if someone is caught in a fault, restore them gently, remembering you could be next. Bear one another's burdens doesn't mean fix other people.
You don't take the weight away.
You stand under it with them.
Christians have lived this in casseroles after funerals, rides to chemotherapy, rent paid quietly, friends who sit with you on the worst night and say almost nothing.
The law of Christ looks a lot like showing up with your end of the couch.

how: Many churches organize meals, visits, rides and prayer for members going through illness, grief or hardship, and many Christians take Galatians 6:2 as a description of what church should be.

o: a tax that Rome charged on every early church
a sin you have to confess before a priest
a heavy load, from a crushing weight to a daily pack

games.q: what's inside the verse — tap the pairs.
p: a daily pack, your own load
arguing over which laws to keep

s: two different Greek words: heavy weights to share in verse two, a personal pack in verse five.
Paul calls bearing burdens the law of Christ
"bear ye one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ."
bearing someone's burden means fixing their problem
you don't take the weight away. you stand under it with them.

games.q: a friend's father has just died. she's overwhelmed. what does Galatians 6:2 point toward?
o: give her advice on how to grieve.
leave her alone: everyone carries their own burden.
show up with a meal and stay a while.
games.why: a crushing weight is meant to be shared. the verse doesn't ask you to fix it, only to get under it with her.

practice: First, notice your own pack, what's simply yours to carry today, and just name it.

Then picture someone you know under a heavy weight right now, illness, grief, money, a child in trouble, a job that's crushing them, and without trying to fix it, ask: where is one corner of this I could lift, a meal, a ride, an hour of childcare, a text that says I'm here?
If you pray, hold them before God.

wordCard.voice: Burden, the word Paul also uses for your own daily load, carried alongside the crushing weights we bear for each other.

orig.note: Greek: heavy weights, burdens (Galatians 6:2), different from phortion, a personal pack (6:5).

carryVoice: Your line: carry each other. Your own pack, and a corner of theirs. See you on day one hundred forty-three.
